heading: Introduction to permaculture
body: Before you dig anything, it helps to know how decisions are made.
This lesson is the foundation of everything else in this course. Three ethics, a list of design principles, and one simple way to arrange your land.
None of them needs money. All of them change where you put things, or how far you walk every day.
Think about your site. Which part do you visit most often?

heading: Why this matters
body: Good design saves work before you pick up a spade.
Most of the effort on a small farm is not planting or harvesting. It is walking, carrying and fixing what was put in the wrong place.
Permaculture is a way of deciding where things are put, so that the land works with you and not against you.
Think about one job on your farm that takes longer than it should. Where does all the time really go?

heading: Learning outcomes
body: At the end of this lesson you will be able to do three things.
Name the three ethics, and use them to make a decision that has no clear answer.
Name the design principles that matter most on your land, and explain why.
Draw your zones and sectors on one page.
This drawing is the backbone of all the plans you will make after this.

heading: Caring for the earth
body: The first ethic is caring for the earth (Earth Care).
This means treating land, water, plants and animals as living systems that we must protect, not as things to use until they are finished.
A system you use up stops giving you a return. A system you protect keeps giving you a return.
Look at one piece of bare ground on your land. Is something protecting it at the moment?

heading: Caring for people
body: The second ethic is caring for people (People Care).
Your family's needs come first, then your community's needs.
A farmer who sells all the eggs and all the vegetables, keeping nothing for the family table, skips Caring for people.
The farm is made to feed the home that works it.
What comes out of your land that your family does not eat?

heading: Sharing fairly
body: The third ethic is sharing fairly (Fair Share).
Take only what you need, and return the surplus to the system: seed, food, water, knowledge.
A farmer who sells all the leftover maize, keeping none for compost or seed, breaks this principle. Nothing goes back.
A community that fences off a shared water source with wire breaks it too.
What does your land get from you in each season of the year?

heading: Watch: one decision, three ethics
body: A borehole serves your home. Neighbours ask for water too.

First find out whether sharing is allowed. Check whether the borehole can serve all users without taking too much water. If sharing is allowed and the water is enough, agree on a fair way of sharing and keep watching the water level. Caring for people and sharing fairly lead the agreement. Caring for the earth means protecting the source. Watching the level alone does not make using more safe or allowed.
Who can help you check the rules and the water available?

heading: When there is no rulebook
body: That is why the ethics really exist.
A neighbour asks to graze his cattle after a drought. A flood damages your swales. Nobody has written the answer down.
The ethics help you weigh up those ways of choosing and explain your decision. Check the rules and ask for permission where it is needed.
Build these three into how you think before you build anything on the land.

heading: Twelve principles
body: David Holmgren set out twelve design principles in the book Essence of Permaculture. Bill Mollison and David Holmgren started the idea of permaculture together.
You do not need all twelve to begin. Three useful places to start in this lesson are these: observe and interact, catch and store energy, and use edges and care for what is at the margins.
We will take those three one at a time.

heading: Observe and interact
body: Look at your land for a full season before you do big digging work.
One storm shows you one moment. A full rainy season shows you a pattern: where the water goes, where it gathers, where it does not reach.

This helps you understand the place. It does not by itself show that a swale is good or safe to build. Before digging, check the land, the slope, the way the water runs down, and a safe way for the overflow to go out that will not cause soil erosion or send water that can damage neighbours. Ask a trained local mentor to check the site.
Where does the water come out on your land? Do you really know, or are you guessing?

heading: Catch and store energy
body: Gather rain, sun and biomass (grass and leaves) before they leave your place.
All of those arrive free and leave free. Water runs away, leaves are blown off by the wind, sun reaches bare ground.
Compare the costs with the work and the benefit on your farm.
Describe one thing that arrives on your land free and then leaves again unused.

heading: Use edges and care for what is at the margins
body: An edge is a place where two things meet: a wire fence line or a string beside a road.
These can be useful places to watch. Look at what is already growing well next to yours. The land itself tells you something.
Which edges on your site are doing nothing at present?

heading: Use and value diversity
body: Use and value diversity. Hail damage to maize depends on the storm and on the stage of the plant's growth. This principle does not promise that the plant will survive in every situation.
Two others you should know: produce no rubbish, so that food scraps become compost and compost becomes soil. And use small and slow solutions: a bucket can water a bed without electricity at all.
What could one bad day cost you now?

heading: Combine in the place of separating
body: Put each thing where it works for its neighbours.

The garden, fruit trees and the chicken area are arranged so that the chickens go round the beds after harvest as a combining. Keep chickens away from crops harvested for eating. Fresh manure can have germs. Ask an agricultural mentor to tell you how to treat the bed safely before edible crops come back. Chickens can remove insects and add richness to the soil instead of sitting doing nothing in a stable kraal.
Three similar things, separated by a fence, do only their own work.
Choose two or three principles that speak to your biggest problem and use them strongly. The others will become clear as you go on.

heading: Zones: planning by how often you visit
body: Zones go from 0 to 5, and are measured by your feet, not by your fence.
Zone 0 is the house. In this example, Zone 1 is near the house and holds herbs and salad leaves harvested often.
Zone 2 is the main garden and the chicken area, visited once or twice a day. Zone 3 is the main field, visited once a week.
Zone 4 is almost wild: fruit trees and livestock feed that needs attention sometimes. Zone 5 is left wild.

heading: Keep daily plants close
body: Herbs that you pick often are easy to look after near the house.
If you put them far away, walking a long time may mean you skip visiting. The herbs may be neglected.
Think about the paths you walk every day.
What do you visit often that could be close?

heading: Zones plan your work
body: This is the purpose of this whole exercise.
Zones help to arrange the place by the effort you spend: the walking, carrying and checking that fill a real day.
What you need often stays close. That can reduce walking and work through the season.
Stand at the kitchen door. What can you reach without thinking?

heading: Sectors: energies that arrive from outside
body: Zones come from inside your land. Sectors come from outside.
Sun, wind, rain, floods and fire all come across your boundary whether you have planned or not.
Look where the strong wind comes from on your farm. Records of a nearby weather station can help you check where the wind comes from. Look where the rainwater enters and goes over your land.
Which side does the damaging weather come from?

heading: Watch: shelter between wind and crops
body: Look at this example. The wind comes from the north-west.
Trees and shrubs stand between this wind and the crops.
Some wind passes through the windbreak. Some goes over it or around its ends.
A shelter can reduce wind speed behind it. The design and care of the windbreak are important.
On your site, observe the damaging winds before you choose where you will plant. This picture is not a planting plan.

heading: Draw it, you will have a design
body: Draw your boundary. Mark the house. Draw circles outward according to how often you visit.
Then draw arrows coming in from outside showing sun, wind, fire and water.
This page is the backbone of your design. Everything else in this course depends on it.
It does not need to be neat. It must be true.

heading: Fieldwork
body: Draw your zones and sectors on one page.
Mark Zone 0 and Zone 1 first, then continue outward as far as your land goes.
Add each arrow of energy that comes from outside, writing where it comes from.
Take a photo of the drawing.

heading: Field action
body: Go out and compare your drawing with the land.
Stand at the kitchen door and count what is really in Zone 1 today.
Find one thing planted further away than how much you use it, and write down where it should be moved to.
Then ask an older neighbour which side the worst wind comes from, and compare his answer with your arrow.
